title: Enterprise Git
description: Adopt Git at scale across large organizations with hosted platforms, access controls, and standardized workflows.

data.text: Moving Git from a developer tool to an enterprise standard means solving problems Git never intended: compliance, audit trails, access control, and cross-team visibility. Hosted Git platforms provide the scaffolding, but you still need policies and conventions to make them work at scale.

GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket each offer enterprise plans with SAML/SSO, audit logs, and fine-grained permissions. Evaluate them on compliance needs, existing identity provider integration, and whether your teams already use CI/CD or issue tracking from the same vendor.

Branch policies enforce who can write to protected branches and what checks must pass before merging. At minimum, protect `main` from direct pushes, require at least one review, and require status checks from CI.

data.title: GitHub branch protection rules (summary)
data.code:
# Configured via GitHub UI or REST API
# Require pull request reviews before merging
# Require status checks to pass
# Require signed commits
# Include administrators in restrictions

data.text: Open-source projects and some enterprises use a fork-based model where contributors clone the repository into their own namespace, work in branches, and open pull requests against the upstream. This isolates production code from contributor write access while keeping contributions reviewable.

For very large teams or air-gapped environments, self-hosted Git servers or GitHub Enterprise Server reduce external dependencies. Ensure backups, monitoring, and access logging are part of the deployment, not afterthoughts.

data.title: Policy over tooling
data.text: A hosted platform with no branch protection rules is just a fancy file server. Invest in written workflows and training before rolling out enterprise Git to hundreds of developers.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Use hosted platforms with SSO, audit logs, and fine-grained permissions.
Protect main branches with review and CI requirements.
Fork-based workflows scale contributor access without exposing production branches.
Self-hosted Git requires the same operational rigor as any production service.
